Response to Reviewers
The authors would like to thank all reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions,
which guided us in significantly improving our manuscript. In the revised manuscript, we
added a section to the Results that describes the SNFL model, along with model figures
(Fig. 8), explaining the importance of this study in proposing the model. Furthermore, we
built a simplified mathematical model that simulates the pacesetting by the SNFL.
Another significant addition in the revised manuscript is the direct evidence of a causal
relationship between the AVP neuronal clock and the short-period behavior rhythm in
VIP-deficient mice (Fig. 3).
Our detailed responses to the reviewers’ concerns are itemized below.
Response to Reviewer #1
1-1. How the 20,000 neurons and astrocytes of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
generate a stable ~24 hours (circadian) signal is an important area of study because this
property determines the temporal pattern of our behavior and physiology. In this study,
Wang et al. use an impressive range of intersectional manipulations and long-term in vivo
Ca-imaging to explore how two distinct cell groups of the SCN, those expressing arginine
vasopressin (AVP) and those expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interact to
main robust rhythmicity. They conclude that “the neuronal feedback circuit composed of
AVP cellular oscillator and VIP peptide signaling is crucial for the robust circadian
rhythm.”
I have two significant thoughts about his study. First, the impressive technical features of
in vivo cell-specific imaging have already been published by this group, including the
excellent paper by Tsuno et al, PLOS Biology, 2023. This reduces some of the immediate
impact of the study. Second, the conclusion could have been made before this work was
conducted. There is an extensive literature, again some of it from this group, about the
role of AVP neurons in driving circadian behavior and of the requirement for VIP
signaling to sustain the SCN clockwork. The real question to be answered is how do AVP
and VIP cells do what they do - what are the mechanisms? It is not clear to me how this
study moves towards a substantial answer, but the Authors may be able to articulate how
their results do push things forward by elucidating “the mechanism of how VIP regulates
the cellular clocks of AVP neurons”.
Response: The authors appreciate the reviewer’s crucial comments. We are glad that the
reviewer does not reject our SNFL model, but rather considers it reasonable and capable
of explaining the previously reported results in an extensive literature. While we, as
well as Prof. Joe Takahashi’s group, have proposed the dominant role of AVP neurons as
the circadian oscillator in vivo and ex vivo, respectively (Mieda et al., Neuron 2015, PMID:
25741730; Mieda et al., Curr Biol 2016, PMID: 27568590; Tsuno et al., Plos Biol 2023,
PMID: 37643163; Shan et al., Neurons 2020, PMID: 32768389), we do not feel that this
view is widely accepted in the field (e.g., Hastings et al., Nat Rev Neurosci 2018; Patton
et al., Nat Commun 2020; Nikhil et al., bioRxiv 2024, PMID: 39713450). Due to the
impactful role of VIP peptide as a critical synchronizer of SCN cells, many researchers
likely still consider VIP neurons as the dominant circadian oscillator in the SCN network,
a notion that has yet to be demonstrated in vivo. We believe that our SNFL model, built
upon previous works and novel findings in this study, bridges the gap between these two
lines of research. Therefore, as explained below, it provides significant conceptual
progress in understanding the neural mechanism of the mammalian central circadian
clock.
We added a section “Neuronal feedback loop model of the SCN explains experimental
result” and a figure (Fig. 8a) to the Results to explain the SNFL model and clarify its
novel points. We also included a simplified mathematical model that simulates the control
of period length by the SNFL (Fig. 8b). Our model combines the new findings from this
study with two lines of previously reported results. First, AVP neurons serve as the
primary pacesetter. The other result is that VIP signaling is essential, though the
contribution of VIP neurons as oscillators is minimal. Qualitatively, VIP release,
controlled by AVP neuronal rhythm, daily amplifies and delays the intrinsically short-
period AVP neuronal rhythm, bringing it close to a 24 h-period, under the free-running
condition in DD (i.e., the endogenous SCN rhythm in the absence of any external
zeitgeber, such as a light pulse). Thus, the model centers on a single, primary, short-period
oscillator (AVP neuron), and feedback signals (VIP signaling), driven by this oscillator,
prolong the endogenous period of the oscillator, thereby modulating the overall SCN
period to 24 hours.
The key novel findings of this study to complete our SNFL model are as follows:
#1: AVP neurons maintain an intrinsically short-period, low-amplitude rhythm in vivo
even in the absence of VIP signaling.
#2: AVP neurons are responsible for the short-period behavior rhythm in VIP-deficient
mice.
#3: VPAC in AVP neurons contributes significantly to the phase delay of the AVP
2
neuronal rhythm.
If it were only such a phase-delay/amplification feedback loop, it would be
straightforward. However, we also obtained the following result:
#4: Attenuated, long-period behavior and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms remain when the AVP
neuronal oscillator is attenuated by VIP deficiency, or AVP neuron-specific disruption of
TTFL or transmitter release.
This #4 suggests that non-AVP cells, including VIP neurons, also function as oscillators,
albeit marginally in the presence of SNFL, which complicates the interpretation. Here,
such weak oscillations are incorporated into the unified SNFL model by considering them
as the default clock state (a term inspired by the default mode network) or background
circadian oscillation (a term inspired by cosmic background radiation). These oscillations
become visible in the absence of SNFL. In mammals, almost every cell throughout the
body has a TTFL, as do all SCN cells. Thus, it is not surprising that weak circadian
rhythms emerge when the primary oscillator (AVP neurons) loses control over the rest of
the SCN cellular oscillators. We incorporate all SNFL components in a mathematical
model by adding a term expressing the phase-delaying effect of VIP to a Kuramoto model
equation of two-oscillator coupling: one strong AVP neuronal oscillator with a short
period and one weak non-AVP cellular oscillator (including VIP neurons) with a long
period (Fig. 8b).
Without this extra term (K = 0), the model alone cannot explain the experimental results
V
of this study. Suppose the ensemble period is set according to a simple coupling of
stronger fast and weaker slow oscillators. In that case, the ensemble period would be
much closer to that of the fast oscillator, which does not fit with the experimental results
(i.e., AVP-Ca2+, ~22.7 h; VIP-Ca2+, ~24.3 h, as the representative of non-AVP cells;
ensemble, ~23.7 h, the Ca2+ and behavioral periods in normal mice). Adding the extra
term replicates the recorded period lengths very well. We would like to emphasize that
the model is based on the values measured by long-term, simultaneous, in vivo recordings
of neuron-type-specific Ca2+ rhythms (i.e., AVP, VIP, or CCK neurons) and behavioral
rhythms, which has been done for the first time in this study. This scheme is quite flexible
in setting the ensemble period by adjusting the phase-delaying power of VIP signaling,
even longer than the long-period weak oscillator (“Besides, the SNFL scheme is highly
flexible in setting the ensemble period by adjusting the phase-delaying power of VIP
signaling (K ), ...” in the Discussion). Therefore, it may be suitable for light entrainment
V
by transiently modifying the VIP signaling intensity and subsequently the ensemble
period to cause phase shifts in both directions.
In our previous report (Tsuno et al., Plos Biol 2023, PMID: 37643163), we proposed that
the cellular circadian period of AVP neurons is the primary determinant (i.e., pacesetter)
of the SCN ensemble period in vivo. This view remains unchanged in this study, albeit
with an update reflecting that the ensemble period length is ~1 h longer than the intrinsic
AVP cellular period due to the phase-delaying effect of VIP signaling (“This view
remained unchanged in this study but was further updated to account for the ensemble
period length...” in the Discussion). We were able to make this update because we
successfully estimated the in vivo intrinsic AVP neuronal period using dual-color fiber
photometry recordings in VIP-deficient mice. In this sense, AVP neurons are not fully
autonomous pacesetters. Rather, they are equipped with feedback neural circuits that
perfect their role as the pacesetter. This idea provides a significant conceptual
advancement.
Indeed, as the reviewer pointed out, there are past reports that suggest a part of the
elements that make up our model. However, as far as we know, no similar model has ever
been proposed. In this study, we identified the final critical pieces that complete our model.
We agree that previous studies have demonstrated the necessity of VIP signaling for
sustaining the SCN clockwork, which served as the starting point of our current study.
VIP application or VIP neuronal activation delays PER2::LUC rhythms in explants (An
et al., J Neurophysiol 2011, PMID: 21389307; Patton et al., Nat Commun 2020, PMID:
32636383) and behavior rhythms in vivo (Mazuski et al., Neuron 2018, PMID: 30017392;
Xie et al., Neuron 2023, PMID: 37172583). However, these effects have primarily been
discussed in the context of light entrainment (“which has been regarded as the
cellular/molecular mechanism of phase-delay by the external light pulse” in the
Discussion). Besides, based on the extensive projection of VIP neurons to the SCN shell
and the high (but not exclusive) expression of VPAC in the shell, researchers postulate
2
that VIP resets the SCN ensemble phase by acting on the SCN shell. Nevertheless, there
is no direct evidence of this, nor of the identity of the direct target cells that mediate the
phase reset among the many VPAC -expressing cells. Some studies have described the
2
reciprocal interaction between the SCN core and shell in the SCN explants, again
primarily in the context of responses to the phase-shifting light pulses, the extreme
photoperiods, and the coupling of shell and core oscillators of comparable strength (Albus
et al., Curr Biol 2005, PMID: 15916945; Evans et al., Neuron 2013, PMID: 24267653;
Myung et al., PNAS 2015, PMID: 26130804).
It should be noted that this model does not exclude the functions of AVP neurons and VIP
neurons as the output arms of the SCN, such as those regulating timed drinking behavior
(Gizowski et al., Nature 2016, PMID: 27680940), neurosecretion via the SCN-OVLT
portal system (Yao et al., Nat Commun 2021, PMID: 34561434), and corticosterone
release (Paul et al., Nat Commun 2020, PMID: 32193397; Jones et al., Nat Commun 2021,
PMID: 34599158). This situation may be analogous to the intracellular timekeeping,
wherein the TTFL ticks the cellular clock and also drives output clock-controlled genes
in individual cells (“However, this model does not exclude the involvement of extra-SCN
neurons, because the SCN also receives inputs from its surroundings” in the Discussion).
We made a maximum effort to clarify the novelty of the current study in the revised
manuscript. However, the reviewer’s instructions and suggestions would be more than
welcome to further improve its readability.
Regarding the reviewer’s comment on the technical features of this study, we feel that it
was undervalued. The other two reviewers agreed that our strategy for this study is
technically novel and excellent. As mentioned earlier, in vivo multicolor measurements
combined with locomotor activity monitoring for over three weeks allowed us to directly
correlate the SCN dynamics and behavior rhythms for the first time, which cannot be
done with SCN explants. Besides, we examined multiple neuron type-specific genetic
manipulations, including AVP neuron-specific Vipr2 knockout, which has not been done
previously.
As the reviewer pointed out, the precise molecular mechanisms of how VIP regulates the
cellular clocks of AVP neurons is the critical question. Given the importance of VPAC
2
in AVP neurons, as demonstrated here, we speculate on the involvement of the cAMP
cascade and Per induction, as has been suggested for light entrainment and VIP effects
on the SCN. Some expected molecular mechanisms, based on the previous reports, were
discussed (“The exact intracellular events downstream of VPAC in AVP neurons to delay
2
their TTFLs remain elusive...” in the Discussion). What exactly is happening in AVP
neurons remains to be determined. However, this will require in vivo analyses, which are
technically more challenging than those using an ex vivo system. Therefore, we would
like to pursue this important topic as the next step in our research.
1-2. Figures 1 & 2 show how Ca2+ rhythms in SCN VIP and AVP cells relate to each other
and to behavioral rhythms in wild-type mice, and then how these relationships possibly
change in the VIP-deficient ViptTA mouse. Specifically, it shows that loss of VIP reduces
the amplitude and shortens the period of AVP Ca rhythms and, in parallel, is associated
with disrupted behavioral activity rhythms with overall shortened period.
Response: In DD, the ability of AVP neurons as the pacesetter is likely around the
threshold due to their attenuated rhythm in the absence of amplification by VIP signaling.
Above the threshold, AVP neurons retain some control over other SCN cells and the
behavior rhythm, thereby pacesetting a short-period rhythm. Below the threshold,
however, AVP neurons lose control over other SCN cells, allowing weak, long-period
rhythms dissociated from AVP neuronal rhythms. We expanded the discussion on this
topic and also clarified it in the model figures and the mathematical model (Fig. 8).
The heterogeneity of the circadian phenotype in VIP-deficient mice is well known, but the
cause is unclear. Thus, our model may propose an explanation for it.
1-3. Even under LD the Ca rhythms of AVP cells are diminished in VIP-null mice. This is
an interesting result because it indicates that, in the absence of VIP, light cannot boost
the AVP Ca rhythms. Thus, loss of normal VIP signaling affects the SCN circuit properties
and the period of AVP cells.
Response: We appreciate the valuable comment. We agree with this point and added the
sentence: “In LD, light may not appropriately entrain and boost the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm in
the absence of VIP.” (in the Results).
1-4. In the absence of VIP, Ca rhythms in VIP cells remain robustly light-driven but
disappear very rapidly on transfer to DD. Why might VIP cells be sensitive to loss of VIP
because scRNAseq has shown that they do not express Vipr2? The Authors suggest this is
an indirect result of the weaker and faster AVP cell rhythms in VIP-null mice, hence the
common period of 23.67 hours for AVP and VIP cells.
Response: We agree with this point and added the sentence “Such a feedback loop circuit
may also explain the observation that the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm quickly attenuated in DD in
the absence of VIP even though VIP neurons express little VPAC .” (in the Discussion).
2
1-5. In the final stages of the study, however, VIP cells are reported to show a longer
period of 24.33 hours in VIP-null mice. I do not fully understand, however, how the VIP
Ca rhythms were analysed. In Figure 1d, e, it petered out after 1 week of DD but in Figure
2 parameters are calculated until days 16 -20. Is it not possible that these parameter
values are meaningless because the rhythms have become so poorly defined? A value may
be calculated for period, but it will come with an error term that may render it not
biologically meaningful. Similarly, the periodograms in Figure 2a suggest a dual
periodicity (early and later?) for VIP Ca rhythms – but how these were calculated and
analysed statistically is not clear. The time-series plots in Figure 2c show the evolution
of the longer period, but the point remains that these rhythms were very poorly defined
and so how much relevance can be placed on this apparent change in period? In addition,
in the moving time series, the same data points are used repeatedly, and then ANOVA is
applied to the means for each 5 days value. I am unclear as to whether this is appropriate
as the measures are not independent, for example 5-9 shares 4 values of 6-10.
Response: In Fig. 1, we characterized the behavior rhythms by actograms and the Ca2+
rhythms by the curve lines of detrended, smoothened jGCaMP7s/jRGECO1a signals, as
described in the Methods. As the reviewer pointed out, we gave up calculating the values
for VIP-Ca2+ after a week in DD because it became too weak and noisy to accurately
analyze by this method. At the same time, we observed the signs of weak rhythms at the
late stage in actograms. Therefore, in Fig. 2, we used the periodogram analysis to extract
such weak rhythms objectively and statistically. We further clarified the procedure in the
manuscript (Results, Methods, and Legends). We agree with the reviewer that such weak
rhythms may not be biologically meaningful. We merely demonstrated the presence of
“statistically significant” rhythms. To clarify this point, we added the following sentences
to the Results and Discussion: “However, the causal relation between these weak VIP-
Ca2+ and behavior rhythms remains unknown,” “their weak, slow Ca2+ rhythm may be a
passive, merely correlated oscillation.” In fact, it was from this point that we came up
with the idea of the background circadian oscillation. In contrast, we confirmed the causal
relationship between the AVP neuronal rhythm and the short-period behavior rhythm in
VIP-deficient mice in the revised manuscript (Fig. 3).
1-6. In addition, in the moving time series, the same data points are used repeatedly, and
then ANOVA is applied to the means for each 5 days value. I am unclear as to whether
this is appropriate as the measures are not independent, for example 5-9 shares 4 values
of 6-10.
Response: We believed that overlapping shifting windows would express the time course
of period changes more precisely. The purpose of these analyses is not to show significant
oscillation at a certain point, but rather, to compare the time course of period changes
between genotypes. Therefore, we did not consider this procedure statistically
inappropriate. Nevertheless, to avoid such a concern, we also analyzed with multiple time
windows without overlap and reached the same conclusion (Supplementary Fig. 1f,g). If
the reviewer prefers this presentation, we would be happy to replace the graphs.
1-7. A final query is why does the later behavioral period track the presumed late period
of the VIP and not the period of the AVP cells (Figure 2c) if AVP cells are the pacesetters?
Over the 20 days of recording the amplitude and period of AVP cells are unchanged and
so it might be expected that their influence over behavior would also be maintained.
Response: As previously mentioned (1-2), the ability of AVP neurons as to act as the
pacesetter is likely around the borderline in VIP-deficient mice. It is not surprising that
the amplitude of the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm gradually reduces in prolonged DD, although it is
maintained. Such a tendency is seen in Fig. 1d and Fig. 2e. It is well known that VIP- or
VPAC2-deficient mice show phenotypic heterogeneity, single short-period or multiple-
period circadian rhythm. The reviewer’s question may be similar to one we are often
asked by researchers: Why do VIP-deficient mice exhibit two types of behavioral
rhythms? The slight difference in AVP neurons’ pacesetting ability may cause such a
spectrum of circadian phenotypes in these mice.
1-8. In the later stages of recording are we simply looking at some non-specific
associations in a clock that is progressively falling apart: behavioral offsets could not
even be defined in the VIP-null mice? In the early stages of DD, where measurements are
much more robust, AVP and VIP cells behave similarly.
Response: As described above (1-5), we agree with the reviewer that the weak, late-onset
VIP-Ca2+ rhythms have no biological meaning. Although AVP- and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms
behave similarly in the early stages, they are attenuated as compared to normal mice,
which may lead to the attenuation of the behavior rhythm as well, and thereby make it
difficult to define behavioral offsets in VIP-deficient mice. To ensure consistency, the
revised Fig. 1 excludes locomotor offset data from the control mice as well.
1-9. I have a technical question regarding the individual period values. Is there some
aspect of the periodogram which causes it to deliver particular fractional values?
For example, Figure 2a has .67 (2/3) and .33 (1/3), as does Figure 3e, alongside .50 (1/2). To
what degree does the doublet for period in VIP-null animals apply to individual animals
and to what degree is it a population measure?
Response: Because the jGCAMP7s/jRGECO1a signal was recorded every 10 minutes,
the Ca2+ rhythm data are in 10-min bins, i.e., 1/6 h. Therefore, we performed periodogram
analyses with 10-min bins. In Fig. 2a, we first averaged the periodograms of individual
mice and identified the primary and secondary peaks of period lengths. For this reason,
the value is a multiple of 1/6 without standard errors. Since the degree of double
periodicity varied from mouse to mouse, we averaged all periodograms to objectively
extract the period lengths. To confirm this result, we also performed the analysis in reverse
order in the revised manuscript. That is, we first calculated the periods for each mouse
and then averaged them (Fig. 2b,c). The detailed values were different, of course, but the
conclusions were the same.
1-10. “These results suggest that VIP neurons may be a subordinate slow oscillator and
exhibit a weak, long-period rhythm that correlates with the behavior rhythm in vivo when
the AVP cellular rhythm is attenuated by VIP deficiency.”
Alternatively, it may be that the loss of VIP in some way alters the intrinsic properties of
VIP cells. Moreover, the Authors do not consider whether changes in the Ca rhythms are
a result of altered behavioral rhythms and not a cause of them.
Response: The authors appreciate this critical comment. As described above (1-5), we
do not aim to claim that the weak oscillation of VIP neurons drives the weak long-period
behavior rhythm.
1-11. 2. To test whether the VIP-null compromise of AVP (shorter period) and VIP cell
(short then long period) rhythms is generalisable across the SCN, Figure 3 describes Ca2+
rhythms in SCN CCK cells and the impact of VIP deletion on them. Again, elegant
intersectional approaches are deployed. In control mice, the CCK cells exhibit a Ca
rhythm, as reported previously. The VIP-null phenotype of VIP cells was replicated with
an independent cohort of mice. Note, is this assumed independence correct, even though
the mice again had identical periods of 22.67 h and 24.33 h (see technical comment above
re. periodogram)? In VIP-null mice the rhythms are initially light-driven and then damp
rapidly on transfer to DD. They do lengthen, but not to the extent seen in Figure 1, raising
uncertainly about the robustness of the late VIP-null phenotype.
Response: The reason that the value is a multiple of 1/6 is the same as explained above
(1-9). We measured different cohorts of VIP-deficient mice between Fig. 1/2 and Fig. 3,
and we think the VIP-null phenotype is consistent. The reviewer may be criticizing the
apparent difference between Fig. 2d and 4g. As the reviewer pointed out, the late VIP-
null rhythmicity varies between individuals, resulting in big error bars. We repeatedly
expressed this rhythm as “weak” and never claimed it was robust. We added a sentence
“Although 5 days may be too short to precisely calculate the period length, it may be
sufficient to briefly track the time course of changing periods” in the Results.
1-12. The Ca rhythms of CCK cells in VIP-null mice were light-driven on LD and showed
rapid damping in DD, replicating the phenotype of VIP cells. They do not, however, show
a late lengthened period, as the VIP cells did, so they are a half-way house. The statistical
comparisons are pretty weak, however, and again suffer from the poor definition/ high
variance of rhythms in the later stages. The Authors conclude that “CCK-Ca2+ rhythm is
weak and unstable and has more heterogeneous periods in VIP deficiency. Such
heterogeneity may partly reflect that CCK neurons contain at least two subpopulations,
one overlapping with a small subpopulation of AVP neurons.” This is speculation.
Fundamentally in the absence of VIP the SCN cellular rhythms are low amplitude (AVP)
or damped poorly defined period (VIP, CCK).
Response: We completely agree with the reviewer that “Fundamentally in the absence of
VIP the SCN cellular rhythms are low amplitude (AVP) or damped poorly defined period
(VIP, CCK).” In the revised manuscript, we demonstrated that the low amplitude AVP
cellular rhythm is responsible for the short-period behavior rhythm in VIP deficient mice
(Fig. 3). As for VIP and CCK cellular rhythms, we clarified that we are showing just
correlations, as explained above (1-5). Concerning subpopulations of CCK neurons, we
added an experiment estimating the overlap of AVP and CCK neurons in the revised
manuscript (Supplementary Fig. 6).
1-13. 3. Given the importance of VIP when absent throughout development, the Authors
then explore the effect of adult-restricted loss of the VIP cells. A different mouse line,
heterozygous VIP IRES Cre received AAV injection of Cre-dependent caspase.
Post-mortem staining revealed absence of VIP, and the mice exhibited a short period of 22.9
hours. Unfortunately, there are no control animals in this experiment: for example,
injected with control AAV or mice not of the IRES-CRE background and injected with
AAV conditional caspase. The data are therefore incomplete, and this particular study
would require expansion to be suitable for publication.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. We added appropriate control mice in
the revised manuscript (Supplementary Fig. 7).
1-14. 4. To complement the examination of VIP-deficiency, the Authors then deleted its
receptor, Vipr2, from AVP cells by cell-specific expression of Cre-conditional CAS9 and
AAV inject of sgRNA. (Figure 4) This is, again, a technically impressive approach
although targeting was confirmed by mCherry and GFP signals but levels of Vipr2 were
not determined. This targeting caused an acute shortening of period, compared to mice
injected with control AAV, but given the impact of genomic ablation of Vipr2 (short period

Response to Reviewer #2
2-1. The study applied dual-color fiber photometry recording to VIP-deficient mice,
allowing them to simultaneously monitor the cellular circadian rhythms from two types
of SCN neurons. They analyzed the circadian behavior rhythms of multiple mouse strains
that had various impairments in the communication between VIP and AVP neurons.
This is an extremely elegant and complex genetic approach, to disrupt VIP (and other)
signaling while performing dual-color Ca2+ fiber photometry. The technological
approach is very impressive. The results are complex. One caveat that should be, and is,
addressed in the text is that the assumption that the populations of VIP and AVP (and
CCK) cells are internally coherent, especially during disruption of normal signaling,
may not be true. For example see https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2209329120. Plus,
recent snRNAseq studies have shown that VIP+ and AVP+ populations are internally
diverse. Therefore, treating them as distinct groups may be an oversimplification. I don’t
suggest that it invalidates these results, just that it should be clearly acknowledged that
there is likely more complexity/diversity among cells and across days. The beginning of
the discussion does acknowledge this, which is good, as it is a key point.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s positive comment. Regarding the diversity of
AVP and VIP neurons, we expanded the discussion in the revised manuscript (the first
paragraph of the “Discussion” section). We acknowledge that recent snRNA-seq studies
have significantly advanced our understanding of SCN neuron heterogeneity, identifying
numerous subpopulations distinguishable by their gene expression profiles. However,
developing genetic tools to specifically manipulate individual subpopulations
necessitates considerable additional effort. Even though such simplification is a limitation
of this study, we believe this research is at the cutting edge of what is currently possible.
Regarding the internal coherence of VIP and AVP neuronal populations, we
(AVP neurons and VIP neurons) and others (VIP neurons) successfully observed
significant daily rhythms of Ca2+ by in vivo fiber photometry. Therefore, it is rational to
conclude that these cells are internally coherent (synchronized) to some extent at the
circadian frequency, despite having certain diversity in phase and amplitude of circadian
oscillation. This should be true even during the disruption of normal signaling, though the
coherence may be further attenuated. Does the reviewer think it’s possible that, in a
coupled system, the population has a rhythm while the individual components have no
rhythm?
Stowie et al. (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2209329120) is an
excellent, elegant, and impressive study, achieving technically challenging single-cell
recordings of Ca2+ rhythms of SCN AVP neurons in free-moving mice. Their conclusion
that most individual AVP neurons do not exhibit circadian baseline Ca2+ rhythms in both
LD and DD somewhat contradicts to our conclusion (“assumption” by the reviewer) of
some circadian coherence between AVP neurons. Even at the population level (mean
fluorescence values for all ROIs), they concluded that AVP neurons do not show a
significant circadian rhythm of intracellular Ca2+ level in DD. On the other hand, and
importantly, they also described that the majority of bootstrap trials, which were
performed to address the unequal contribution of cells from each mouse, suggested a
population-level circadian rhythm in both LD and DD. This bootstrap result might suggest
that there was a significant difference in the quality of single-cell recordings between
individual mice used. Thus, their data do not necessarily deny the population-level
circadian rhythm in AVP neurons.
Even regarding the single cell-level rhythm, what we failed to grasp in their
paper is as follows. Fig. 1A reported that only 6 out of 26 cells demonstrated significant
rhythmicity in DD in the intensity of GCaMP signals. On the other hand, Supplemental
Table S1 lists all cells recorded. Among 50 cells recorded in DD, 23 cells showed
significant rhythmicity in the intensity of GCaMP signals. Intriguingly, 15 cells recorded
in a mouse included 4 rhythmic cells, 11 cells in the second mouse included 2 rhythmic
cells, and 24 cells in the third mouse included 17 rhythmic cells. Thus, we were not sure
which of the 23 cells in Fig. 1A corresponded to which cells in Table S1. Moreover, we
also wondered about the substantial differences among the three recorded mice in the
number of recorded cells and the proportion of rhythmic cells.
Besides, Xie et al. (Neuron 2023, PMID: 37172583) reported the in vivo
circadian rhythm of Fos expression, which often reflects the intracellular Ca2+ level, in
SCN AVP neurons. Although Enoki et al. (PNAS 2017, PMID: 28270612) reported robust
circadian Ca2+ rhythms in individual AVP neurons of SCN explants, results by Stowie et
al. might indicate that in vivo conditions drastically destabilize and attenuate Ca2+
rhythms in each AVP neuron. Nevertheless, it is hard to imagine that there is rhythm at
the population level but no rhythm at all at the individual cell level. At the same time, the
rhythm in individual cells could be buried in noise due to the low signal-to-noise ratio
caused by the technical difficulty of the single-cell recording. While we recognize the
limitation of our current study, as described above and in the first paragraph of the
Discussion in the manuscript, there might be some confounding factors in Stowie et al.,
including the small number of cells recorded, low expression level of GCaMP7s (the
strain Avp-ires2-Cre used has been known for low level expression of Cre and reduction
of endogenous Avp expression: Cheng et al., J Biol Rhythms 2019, PMID: 31452438),
lower sampling frequency (every 3-h recording), and the short-term (2 days) recording.
We discussed the apparent discrepancy between their and our studies in the second
paragraph of the Discussion.
2-2. The results are, generally, wide in terms of # of manipulations, but shallow, in terms
of #s of mice or depth of understanding of the system, derived from a disrupting VIP
signaling, blocking the TTFL in cell subtypes, etc. Studying the coupled system in vivo,
while it is broken, is tough to do before we understand how it works when it isn’t broken.
The discussion reveals that the paper raises way more questions than it can answer.
Overall this is a technical tour de force, with rather limited new insight achieved. No new
conceptual model is provided that can help us understand this circuit better than we
already did.
Response: We provided model figures and further built a simplified mathematical model
to clarify the new idea derived from this study (Fig. 8). We described in detail the new
insight and conceptual advance made by the current study in our response to the first
comment by Reviewer #1. Because it is very long, we will not repeat it here, but ask the
reviewer to look at the communication as well (1-1).
We agree with the reviewer’s opinion, “Studying the coupled system in vivo,
while it is broken, is tough to do before we understand how it works when it isn’t broken.”
On the other hand, comparing the broken system with the intact system is often very
powerful to understand the complicated intact system, such as studying knockout mice to
understand the function of a gene of interest. Otherwise, observing only the intact systems
tends to be just descriptive, without elucidating the causal relationships. Indeed,
recordings in VIP-deficient mice successfully dissolved the stable, fast AVP neuronal
oscillator and weak, slow non-AVP cellular oscillators, owing to the elimination of the
linkage between multiple oscillators. Our new techniques provided key findings essential
for proposing the SNFL model, which has not been presented before. The reviewers'
comments make critical points, but they also seem overly demanding for a single paper.
This research has certainly raised many new questions, and we hope to gain a deeper
understanding of the mechanisms of the SCN central clock by seeking answers to these
questions in the future.
Regarding the number of mice analyzed, we increased the number of mice
recorded in Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7. Because long-term in vivo fiber photometry
recordings are technically much more difficult than simple behavior rhythm recordings,
we think that the number of mice used in this study is acceptable (e.g., n=3 for some
experiments in Xie et al., Neuron 2023, PMID: 37172583).
Response to Reviewer #3
3-1. Summary of the key results
The researchers investigated the role AVP neurons play in SCN regulation. They
hypothesize that VIP -> AVP communication plays a role in circadian rhythm, given that
the TTFL loop in VIP neurons is weaker compared to that in AVP neurons. The research
shows that AVP neurons are the principal oscillators with an intrinsically short period. It
strengthens previous observations by this research group. When the internal clock of AVP
neurons is disrupted by Bmal1 KO or their communication with other neurons is removed
with TeNT, the rhythm becomes longer than 24 hours. These results shed interesting new
light on the role of AVP neurons.
I think the interpretation of some unique features that appeared in the results could be
claimed in a better way if additional data will be considered and presented, as listed
below.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments.
3-2. Originality and significance:
The paper, as indicated in the discussion, is the first to use fiberphotometry with 2-colors
in the SCN in vivo. The paper nicely combines genetic manipulation and AAV-based
technologies (such as CRISPR) with calcium imaging and LMA (locomotor activity)
detection. Furthermore, the paper’s significance lies in the in vivo monitoring of AVP-
related features.
The fact that in vivo effects are different from slices is critical here, as the SCN and AVP
neurons also get inputs from the surrounding, which was not tested or discussed here,
which is a weakness of the paper.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. We added a discussion about
this point in the revised manuscript: “Because AVP and VIP neurons are reciprocally
connected directly and indirectly, the intra-SCN network may be sufficient for SNFL
function. However, this model does not exclude the involvement of extra-SCN neurons,
because the SCN also receives inputs from its surroundings.”
3-3. The paper aims to understand the communication mechanism, but it lacks a clear
model, or at least it is not represented in a clear way. To specify, the fact that AVP is a
short-period pacemaker is well explained and demonstrated, but the interpretation of the
changes in the LMA split or VIP calcium imaging after 3 weeks is not strongly convincing.
An additional figure that shows the model will be a great addition.
Response: We added model figures and a brief mathematical model to explain the results
and our idea better (Fig. 8). Regarding LMA (locomotor activity) split, we previously
demonstrated that the lack of GABA release from AVP neurons, due to specific Vgat
deletion, causes LMA split (expansion of the activity time), without changing the free-
running period (Maejima et al., PNAS 2021, PMID: 33526663). In these mice, the TTFL
and AVP-Ca2+ rhythms in the SCN appeared normal, but the phase relationships between
AVP-Ca2+ and circadian morning (M) / evening (E) locomotor activities were
significantly altered. Thus, GABAergic transmission of AVP neurons contributes to the
phase-setting of LMA. Because both the pacesetting and phase-setting functions of AVP
neurons were impaired in Avp-Bmal1−/− and Avp-TeNT mice, the LMA rhythm
demonstrated both long period and split. The observation that the split was more severe
in Avp-TeNT than Avp-Vgat−/− may indicate the involvement of transmitters other than
GABA in the phase-setting. At the same time, the existence of both E and M locomotor
activities in many Avp-TeNT mice, albeit split, suggests that AVP neurons are unlikely to
contain neurons (or E and M oscillators) that send the timed output signals to the
locomotion center. Rather, AVP neurons may transmit the timing information to output
neurons, indicating when locomotor activity should occur. We also agree with the
reviewer’s comment on the late-onset VIP-Ca2+ rhythm and LMA. As described in the
response to Reviewer #1 (1-5), we do not aim to claim the causal relation between these
two. We expanded these discussions in the revised manuscript (the paragraph starting with
“TeNT expression in AVP neurons not only lengthened the free-running period but also
altered the phase relationship of E and M locomotor activities….” in the Discussion).
We recognize that how the SCN regulates E and M LMA is a fundamental question in the
field. We would like to pursue this issue further, starting with the phase-setting function
of AVP neurons. It should be noted that the phase-setting mechanism of AVP neurons is
still compatible with the encoding of photoperiod by the phase distribution of SCN clock
neurons (the second-to-last sentence in the same paragraph).
3-4. Data & methodology:
1. The combined usage of calcium imaging, LMA detection, and cell manipulation using
AAV is impressive. The data analysis is straightforward, but could benefit from a more
advanced analysis, which will highlight the dual activity along the day, such as Rayleigh
plots, as presented in Supp. Figure 2.
Response: We may be misinterpreting the reviewer’s point. We could show Rayleigh
plots in Supplementary Fig. 1 for the initial days in DD when the Ca2+ and behavior
rhythms in VIP -deficient mice were relatively coherent. However, it was difficult to run
the same analyses at the late stage in DD because VIP-Ca2+ rhythms were so weak and
noisy.
3-5. 2. In the paper by Wen et. al. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-020-0586-x)
it was shown that Cck neurons are divided into two subpopulations, one is rhythmic
Cck+/C1ql3+ and one is less (Cck+/Bdnf+). Did you try to identify which subpopulation
was located under the fiber? See, for example, https://www.cell.com/cell-
reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(21)01197-9, or even regular slice histology. This could shed
light on the effect found in vivo.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising an important point. The method developed
by Kahan et al. (Cell Rep 2021, PMID: 34592157) presents an elegant strategy for
localizing the optic fibers and GRIN lenses in single-cell Ca2+ imaging, where the depth
of focus planes is shallow. In our fiber photometry, in contrast, the optic fibers were
intended to be positioned just dorsal to the SCN to capture light from the wide area of the
SCN. Therefore, it seems challenging to discriminate between two subpopulations of
CCK neurons solely according to the fiber position. Practically, the CCK-Ca2+ signal was
likely derived from the mixture of these two. Instead, we added data about how much
AVP and CCK neurons overlap in the SCN in the revised manuscript (Supplementary Fig.
6). We conceived this analysis from the data by Wen et al. (Nat Neurosci 2020, PMID:
32066983), indicating a low level Avp expression in the Cck+/C1ql3+ subpopulation.
These data would help clarify the molecular characteristics of CCK neuronal populations
recorded in this study.

acceptable (e.g., n=3 for some experiments in Xie et al., Neuron 2023, PMID: 37172583).

(https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0748730414549767) and AVP single-cell

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The central circadian clock of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) comprises a network of diverse neuronal and glial cell types, yet its operating mechanism remains elusive. Here, by monitoring cellular calcium rhythms in vivo using dual-color fiber photometry in mice lacking vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), we demonstrate that arginine vasopressin (AVP) neurons oscillate intrinsically with a short period and reduced amplitude. This indicates that VIP normally amplifies and phase-delays the AVP neuronal rhythm each day, thereby lengthening its period to approximately 24 h in constant darkness. Consistently, the behavioral circadian period is shortened by AVP neuron-specific VIP receptor dysfunction and lengthened by AVP neuron-specific blockade of neurotransmitter release. VIP neurons and other SCN cell types occasionally exhibit weak, unstable, long-period calcium rhythms only when the AVP neuronal oscillation is attenuated due to VIP deficiency or AVP neuron-specific Bmal1 deletion. Given that AVP neurons serve as the primary pacesetter cells of the SCN ensemble rhythm, these results indicate that an SCN neuronal feedback loop (SNFL), composed of the AVP cellular oscillator and VIPergic signaling, is essential for generating robust circadian rhythms.

---

## Introduction

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the central circadian pacemaker in mammals, orchestrating multiple circadian rhythms of behavior and physiological function according to the environmental light/dark (LD) cues conveyed from the eye1–4. The SCN contains ~20,000 cells, most of which can generate circadian oscillations. In individual cells, the circadian rhythm is driven by the autoregulatory transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) consisting of clock genes such as Per1/2/3, Cry1/2, Bmal1, and Clock1,2. Notably, the TTFL is not unique to SCN cells and is common to almost all peripheral cells2,5. Rather, the SCN constructs a network of many TTFL-driven cellular clocks to generate a highly robust and coherent circadian rhythm as the central clock, which entrains a large number of peripheral clocks throughout the body1–4. Thus, intercellular communication among SCN clock cells through the neuronal and diffusible network distinguishes the SCN from the peripheral clocks. However, the network mechanism underlying the SCN central clock remains unclear.

The SCN is a heterogeneous structure composed of multiple types of neurons and glial cells1–4. Most SCN neurons are GABAergic, and several populations of these GABAergic neurons also co-express neuropeptides. These include arginine vasopressin (AVP)-producing neurons located predominantly in the dorsomedial part (SCN shell) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP)-producing neurons in the ventrolateral part (SCN core). VIP is the most important contributor to the maintenance and synchrony of SCN cellular clocks with varying periods6,7. Therefore, mice deficient in VIP (Vip−/−) or its receptor VPAC2 (Vipr2−/−) demonstrate a drastic attenuation of the free-running rhythm in constant darkness (DD) with a shortened period or unstable multiple periods. In the latter, the free-running period changes suddenly or two periods emerge simultaneously6,8–10. VIP neurons receive direct projections from the retina, are involved in the photoentrainment, and send dense projections dorsally to the SCN shell1,9,11. However, the precise mechanisms by which VIP regulates SCN circuit remain incompletely understood.

On the other hand, our studies and those of others have suggested that the TTFL-driven cellular clocks in AVP neurons may play a dominant role than those of other SCN neurons in the generation of circadian oscillation by the SCN network, regulating the circadian oscillation of other cells and setting the SCN ensemble period3. Thus, AVP neuron-specific disruption of the TTFL by deleting Bmal1 (Avp-Bmal1−/− mice) results in an unstable, attenuated free-running rhythm with a lengthened period and the activity time (the interval between the onset and offset of locomotor activity)12–16. Furthermore, the cellular period length of AVP neurons appears to be the primary determinant of the SCN ensemble period16,17. In contrast, similar genetic manipulations of disrupting the TTFL or altering the cellular period in VIP neurons have little effect on the amplitude and period of the free-running behavior rhythm13–16,18, suggesting that VIP peptide is critical but the TTFL in VIP neurons may be dispensable for the circadian timekeeping. Besides, our previous studies indicated the importance of in vivo analysis of SCN network dynamics16,17.

Thus, there is a functional differentiation between the shell and the core within the SCN network. However, how the two integrate to generate the circadian rhythm of the SCN ensemble is still unclear. In the current study, we investigated the regulation of AVP neuronal circadian oscillation by VIP in vivo. To this end, we applied dual-color fiber photometry recording to VIP-deficient mice, allowing us to simultaneously monitor the cellular circadian rhythms from two types of SCN neurons. We then analyzed the circadian behavior rhythms of multiple mouse strains that had various impairments in the communication between VIP and AVP neurons. Our results reveal a feedback loop neuronal circuit of these two neuron types that may be the essential network mechanism of the SCN central circadian pacemaker.

---

## Results

AVP neurons maintain a short-period Ca2+ rhythm in VIP-deficient mice
To elucidate the mechanism of how VIP regulates the cellular clocks of AVP neurons, we first aimed to compare the circadian rhythm of intracellular Ca2+ in SCN AVP neurons between control and VIP-deficient mice. Intracellular Ca2+ rhythms are a nice measure of cellular circadian rhythms in vivo that can be recorded in a neuron type-specific manner11,16,19–21. We used the homozygous Vip-tTA knock-in mice (ViptTA/tTA), which are equivalent to Vip knock-out mice and exhibit a spectrum of phenotypes such as simple short-period or complicated multiple-period behavioral rhythms10. In addition, their specific expression of tTA in VIP neurons allowed us to record Ca2+ rhythms in SCN AVP and VIP neurons (AVP- and VIP-Ca2+) separately and simultaneously when combined with hemizygous Avp-Cre BAC transgenic mice12. Thus, we generated VIP-deficient Avp-Cre; ViptTA/tTA mice and heterozygous control Avp-Cre; Vipwt/tTA mice and then targeted the expression of green (jGCaMP7s)22 and red (jRGECO1a)23 fluorescent Ca2+ sensor proteins in AVP and VIP neurons, respectively, by simultaneous injection of Cre- and tTA-dependent AAV vectors (AAV-CAG-FLEX-jGCaMP7s and AAV-TRE-jRGECO1a) (Fig. 1a, b).

In vivo dual-color fiber photometry with simultaneous monitoring of spontaneous locomotor activity revealed robust, temporally coordinated AVP- and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms in control mice in both light/dark (LD) and dark/dark (DD), higher during the (subjective) day (Fig. 1c–e and Supplementary Fig. 1a–c). In VIP-deficient mice, the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm was comparable to that of controls in LD but rapidly attenuated in DD, even when the locomotor activity still showed rhythmicity (Fig. 1c, e and Supplementary Fig. 2). This made it difficult to determine the daily onset and offset of the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm from its waveforms after a week in DD (Fig. 1e–g). The number of jRGECO1a-expressing cells was comparable between control and VIP-deficient mice (Supplementary Fig. 1e), suggesting that the lack of VIP did not decline the VIP neuronal health. In contrast, the amplitude of the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm was substantially reduced in both LD and DD, but it remained stable in DD (Fig. 1c, d and Supplementary Fig. 2). Consistent with the changes in the behavior rhythm, the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm showed a phase advance in LD (midpoint phase: control, ZT 4.11±0.38; VIP-deficient, ZT 21.62±0.80, p<0.001) and a shortened period in DD (control, ~23.7 h; VIP-deficient, ~22.5 h, p<0.05) (Fig. 1f, g and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Notably, the latter was almost identical to the short free-running period of the behavior rhythm (determined based on the locomotor activity onsets), even when behavior changed to a long-period rhythm later in DD (Fig. 1c, g and Supplementary Fig. 2). These results suggest that AVP neurons intrinsically oscillate with a short period and that VIP enhances and delays the oscillation of AVP neurons to make their period closer to 24 h in DD. In turn, the enhanced AVP neuronal rhythm may confer a robust circadian oscillation of VIP neurons, regulating the timing of VIP release. In LD, light may be unable to appropriately entrain and boost the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm in the absence of VIP.

In this study, we used mice of both sexes and analyzed them collectively. However, we confirmed that the results remain fundamentally unchanged when analyzing males and females separately (e.g., Supplementary Fig. 3; also see “Animals” in the “Methods”). The sex of each mouse is disclosed in the Supplementary Figs. and the Source Data file.

VIP-Ca2+ changes to a weak, long-period rhythm in VIP-deficient mice
In VIP-deficient mice, the period length of AVP-Ca2+ rhythm was comparable with the short-period behavior rhythm in DD. As a result, in more than half of VIP-deficient mice, the AVP-Ca2+ rhythm dissociated from the long-period behavior rhythm in the later stage of DD. The VIP-Ca2+ rhythm in actograms initially followed the short-period AVP-Ca2+ and behavior rhythms but gradually disappeared and became very weak and noisy in DD (Fig. 1c–g and Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). Considering the multiple periodicities of the behavior rhythm in VIP-deficient mice6,8–10, we performed periodogram analyses of Ca2+ rhythms throughout three consecutive weeks in DD to detect weak rhythms with different periods objectively and quantitatively. The VIP-Ca2+ rhythm demonstrated two period peaks in most VIP-deficient mice (Supplementary Fig. 2). Averaging periodograms of all the recorded VIP-deficient mice clarified two peaks in the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm, a primary short period (22.67 h) and a secondary long period (24.33 h), whereas AVP-Ca2+ rhythm showed only one short period (22.50 h) (Fig. 2a; period values are multiple of 1/6 because of 10-min bins of Ca2+ recordings). In contrast, both AVP- and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms of control mice presented a robust single period within the normal range (23.67 h), which matched that of the behavior rhythm (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 1a). We obtained a similar result by first detecting two period peaks for each mouse and then calculating the mean values for the short and long periods of each mouse (AVP-Ca2+: control, 23.60±0.09 h; VIP-deficient, 22.61±0.07 h; VIP-Ca2+: control, 23.60±0.09 h; VIP-deficient primary, 22.67±0.08 h; secondary, 24.23±0.13 h) (Fig. 2b, c).

To determine the stage of DD at which the secondary long period occurred, we next calculated the time courses of amplitudes (Qp) and periods of AVP-Ca2+, VIP-Ca2+, and behavior rhythms by sequential periodogram analyses with 5-day shifting windows. Although 5 days may be too short to precisely calculate the period length, it may be sufficient to briefly track the time course of changing periods. In VIP-deficient mice, the peak Qp values of the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm decreased continuously during the first 7–8 days (early stage) and then sustained at a relatively low value until the end of the recording (late stage) (Fig. 2e, right). At the early stage, there was no significant difference in the period length between AVP-Ca2+, VIP-Ca2+, and behavior rhythms (Fig. 2d, right). At the late stage, however, the period of the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm was lengthened close to the long period of the behavior rhythm (VIP-Ca2+ vs. Locomotor activity, p>0.99), whereas the AVP-Ca2+ period remained short (AVP-Ca2+ vs. VIP-Ca2+, p<0.01; AVP-Ca2+ vs. Locomotor activity, p<0.001, Fig. 2d, right and Supplementary Fig. 2). In control mice, all periods of Ca2+ and behavior rhythms were stable and consistent (Fig. 2d, e, right and Supplementary Fig. 1a). These results suggest that VIP neurons may be a subordinate slow oscillator and exhibit a weak, long-period rhythm that correlates with the behavior rhythm period in vivo when the AVP cellular rhythm is attenuated by VIP deficiency. However, the causal relationship between these weak VIP-Ca2+ and behavior rhythms remains unknown.

AVP neurons are responsible for the short-period behavior rhythm in VIP-deficiency
As described above, we observed a correlation between the AVP-Ca2+ and the short-period behavior rhythms in VIP-deficient mice (Figs. 1g and 2d). To test for the causal relationship, we measured the behavior rhythm of VIP-deficient mice with an artificially lengthened TTFL period in AVP neurons due to the specific deletion of the casein kinase 1 delta (CK1δ) gene (Avp-Cre; CK1δflox/flox; ViptTA/tTA = Avp-CK1δ−/−; ViptTA/tTA mice).

As reported previously17, control mice (Avp-CK1δ−/−; Vipwt/tTA) exhibited a robust free-running rhythm in DD with a lengthened period (24.70±0.05 h) (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). In contrast, Avp-CK1δ−/−; ViptTA/tTA mice showed an attenuated behavior rhythm with unstable periods, the mean of which was significantly shorter than that of control Avp-CK1δ−/− mice (24.23±0.11 h) (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 4b). However, unlike CK1δ-intact VIP-deficient mice (Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 2), they never initiated the free-running rhythm with a short period around 22.6 h (Fig. 3a, b, e and Supplementary Fig. 4b). These results indicate that the AVP cellular period regulates the short-period component of the behavior rhythm in VIP-deficient mice.

Ca2+ rhythm of CCK neurons in VIP-deficient mice rapidly attenuates in DD
Next, we aimed to know how unique the consistently short-period AVP-Ca2+ and the late-onset, weak, long-period VIP-Ca2+ rhythms are. In particular, CCK neurons enriched in the anterior shell region of the SCN were of interest as another candidate for a long-period oscillator, because they reportedly play an important role in the behavior under a long-day photoperiod, and their ablation slightly shortened the behavioral free-running period in DD19.

To test this possibility, we introduced a Cck-ires-Cre allele24 to VIP-deficient (Cckwt/ires-Cre; ViptTA/tTA) and control (Cckwt/ires-Cre; Vipwt/tTA) mice and labeled CCK and VIP neurons with jGCaMP7s and jRGECO1a, respectively, by injecting AAV vectors into the SCN (Fig. 4a, b). Our fiber photometry recording successfully recapitulated the reported CCK-Ca2+ rhythm in control mice, with its peak in the second half of the (subjective) day (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 5a)19. In VIP-deficient mice, the CCK-Ca2+ rhythm was robust in LD but rapidly attenuated in DD, as did VIP-Ca2+ (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 5b). However, in contrast to the VIP-Ca2+, the averaged periodogram of the CCK-Ca2+ rhythm for 3-week recordings in DD showed only one period peak (22.00 h), which was even slightly shorter than that of AVP-Ca2+ (22.50 h) but with a broad distribution of significant period lengths on the long-period side up to ~24.3 h, i.e., the secondary peak of the VIP-Ca2+ period (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 5b). Sequential periodogram analysis revealed that the CCK-Ca2+ rhythm gradually reduced its amplitude (Qp) and maintained a short period on average, but with a large variability (Fig. 4g, h and Supplementary Fig. 5b). In contrast, in control mice, CCK-Ca2+, VIP-Ca2+, and behavioral periods were stable and consistent (23.50 h) (Fig. 4f–h and Supplementary Fig. 5a). These results suggest that the CCK-Ca2+ rhythm in VIP deficiency is weak and includes more heterogeneous periods in DD. Furthermore, the late-onset, weak, long-period rhythm is unlikely to be unique to VIP neurons. Rather, it may be a more general feature of the multiple types of SCN cells that appear when AVP neuronal rhythm is attenuated due to VIP deficiency.

Such heterogeneity may partly reflect that CCK neurons contain at least two subpopulations, one overlapping with a small subpopulation of AVP neurons25,26. To estimate the overlap of AVP and CCK neurons, we mated Cck-ires-Cre mice with Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato (Ai14) reporter mice to label CCK neurons with tdTomato27. Then, we stained their SCN sections with an anti-AVP antibody. Approximately 30% of tdTomato+ cells were also AVP+, whereas ~20% of AVP+ cells were tdTomato+ (Supplementary Fig. 6). These AVP-positive and -negative CCK neurons may correspond to Cck+/C1ql3+ and Cck+/Bdnf1+ cells, respectively, reported by Wen et al.25. Thus, the CCK-Ca2+ rhythm recorded here by fiber photometry likely derived from a mixture of these two CCK neuron subpopulations.

Ablating VIP neurons in adulthood causes a simple short-period rhythm
VIP-deficient ViptTA/tTA mice free-ran initially with a short period in DD, but about 60% of the mice changed the free-running rhythm to a long period after 1–2 weeks (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 5). This observation was consistent with the previous reports6,8,9. On the other hand, mice in which VIP neurons were ablated in adulthood were reported to retain the wheel running rhythm but with a shortened period (~22.7 h)28. We also performed a similar experiment to measure the locomotor activity (home cage activity) rhythm by injecting an AAV vector expressing activated Caspase 3 in a Cre-dependent manner (AAV-CAG-FLEX-taCasp3-TEVp) bilaterally into the SCN of Vipwt/ires-Cre mice24. We obtained a similar result, i.e., a shortened free-running period and reduced amplitude of the rhythm (22.77±0.09 h vs. 23.67±0.04 h, p<0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 7). We observed an apparent sex difference in the amplitude reduction but not in the shortening of the period in VIP neuron-ablated mice (Supplementary Fig. 7e, f). These results suggest that VIP neurons contribute to circadian timekeeping by lengthening the circadian period and promoting the rhythmicity in adults. Some compensatory mechanisms may cause multiple periods in VIP-deficient mice during development28.

VPAC2 dysfunction in AVP neurons acutely shortens the free-running period
We next investigated the importance of VIP/VPAC2 signaling in AVP neurons for the pacesetting of the SCN network. We used in vivo genome editing to selectively disrupt the Vipr2 gene in AVP neurons. First, we crossed Avp-Cre mice with Rosa26-LSL-SpCas9 mice, which express SpCas9 Cre-dependently29. We then injected AAV vectors expressing gRNAs targeting the Vipr2 (AAV-U6-gVipr2-EF1α-DIO-mCherry, Avp-Vipr2−/− mice) or control gRNAs (AAV-U6-gControl-EF1α-DIO-mCherry) bilaterally into the SCN of Avp-Cre; Rosa26-LSL-SpCas9 mice (Fig. 5a, b). Substantial reduction of VPAC2 expression specific to the SCN shell was confirmed in Avp-Vipr2−/− mice by immunohistochemistry (Fig. 5b, c).

Avp-Vipr2−/− mice free-ran with a period significantly shorter than controls when released into DD (23.21±0.05 h vs. 23.73±0.05 h, p<0.001) (Fig. 5d, f and Supplementary Fig. 8b). Surprisingly, however, after a while, Avp-Vipr2−/− mice suddenly changed their free-running period to the one comparable to controls (23.85±0.03 h vs. 23.71±0.03 h, p=0.27). This observation led us to start recording locomotor activity immediately after the AAV injection in most of the mice examined, with recordings in LD only for 3 days before DD (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Strikingly, all Avp-Vipr2−/− mice exhibited changes in the free-running period around 21 days after AAV injection. Control mice never showed such a sudden change in the free-running period (Fig. 5d, f and Supplementary Fig. 8a). These results suggest that disruption of VIP/VPAC2 signaling in AVP neurons in adulthood acutely shortens the free-running period due to the reduced phase-delaying effect of VIP on the intrinsic short period of AVP neuronal clocks. On the other hand, the period shortening in Avp-Vipr2−/− mice was less than in VIP-deficient and VIP neuron-ablated mice (23.21±0.05 h vs. 22.67±0.08 h and 22.77±0.09 h). Moreover, the shortening was abolished ~3 weeks after the blockade of the VIP→AVP neuron axis. These observations may be due to an incomplete elimination of VPAC2 from AVP neurons. In addition, we speculate that the indirect pathways may exist that mediate the regulation of AVP neurons by VIP neurons and are involved in the compensatory recovery of the standard period in Avp-Vipr2−/− mice.

Disrupting TTFLs in AVP neurons leaves an attenuated, long-period VIP-Ca2+ rhythm
We previously reported that Bmal1 deletion specific to AVP neurons (Avp-Cre; Bmal1flox/flox = Avp-Bmal1−/− mice) leaves an attenuated circadian behavior rhythm with a lengthening of the free-running period and the activity time12. In contrast, mice become completely arrhythmic when Bmal1 is deleted in all SCN neurons using forebrain-specific CamKII-Cre driver mice16,30. These results may be explained by the weak circadian oscillators of SCN non-AVP cells with a long period as a population in vivo, including VIP and CCK neurons as described above. To test this possibility, we recorded AVP-Ca2+ and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms in Avp-Bmal1−/− mice. To do so, we generated Avp-Bmal1−/−; Vipwt/tTA mice and injected AAV vectors into the SCN (Fig. 6a, b). Similar fiber photometry recordings from Avp-Cre (Bmal1wt/wt); Vipwt/tTA mice (Figs. 1 and 2) were regarded as controls. As expected, the AVP-Ca2+ exhibited little circadian rhythmicity (Fig. 6c, d, f and Supplementary Fig. 9b, c) in Avp-Bmal1−/−; Vipwt/tTA mice. Notably, the VIP-Ca2+ retained a rhythm with a long period (24.54±0.16 h) that is consistent with the period of the behavior rhythm (24.47±0.16 h) in DD (Fig. 6e–g and Supplementary Fig. 9b, c). The duration of high VIP-Ca2+ in the subjective day was compressed according to the prolongation of the activity time of the behavior rhythm (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 9b). Consistent with the previous report12, one out of six Avp-Bmal1−/−; Vipwt/tTA mice demonstrated the multiple period phenotype. In this mouse, the VIP-Ca2+ rhythm was significant but largely attenuated (Supplementary Fig. 9b, mouse #6). These results support the idea that an attenuated oscillation of non-AVP cells with a long period on average manifests in the circadian behavior rhythm when the AVP cellular clock is disrupted.

Blocking neurotransmitter release from AVP neurons lengthens the free-running period
To further explore the evidence that AVP neurons act as the principal oscillator with an intrinsically short period, but its attenuation uncovers a weak, long-period circadian oscillation of non-AVP cells, we next examined the behavioral changes in mice in which the neurotransmitter release from AVP neurons was blocked by AAV-mediated expression of tetanus toxin light chain (Avp-TeNT mice, AAV-EF1α-DIO-GFP::TeNT injected bilaterally into the SCN of Avp-Cre mice) (Fig. 7a, b). Avp-TeNT mice showed a longer free-running period (24.48±0.06 h) in DD than control EGFP-expressing mice (23.28±0.06 h, p<0.001, Fig. 7c–e and Supplementary Fig. 10). These data further confirmed that AVP neurons intrinsically encode a short-period circadian rhythm. The amplitude of the locomotor activity rhythm (periodogram Qp) was not significantly different between groups (p=0.86, Fig. 7d, e). However, individual Avp-TeNT mice exhibited diverse daily patterns of locomotor activity that deviated significantly from the normal nocturnal and bimodal pattern with clear evening (E) and morning (M) locomotor activities (Fig. 7c and Supplementary Fig. 10b). To our surprise, many Avp-TeNT mice showed varying degrees of diurnal locomotor activity rhythms in both LD and DD. To understand the underlying cause, we followed the time course of the emergence of apparent diurnal rhythms in LD after the onset of TeNT expression. Interestingly, TeNT expression in AVP neurons rapidly altered the coupling of E and M locomotor activities (Supplementary Fig. 10c). Namely, Avp-TeNT mice quickly exhibited a prolonged activity time, specifically manifested as a slight advancement in locomotor activity onset (E activity) and a significant delay in locomotor activity offset (M activity). A new steady state of the M-E (M is closer to the following E than to the preceding E) phase relation, rather than the normal E-M phase relation, generated an apparent diurnal behavior rhythm in some mice. Such features can be regarded as a more severe phenotype of the lengthened activity time observed in Avp-Bmal1−/− and Avp-Vgat−/− mice12,20. It should be noted that the free-running period was consistently lengthened in Avp-TeNT mice regardless of their diverse daily patterns of locomotor activity. Thus, these data suggest that blocking neurotransmission of AVP neurons impairs both the pacesetting of the ensemble period and the phase-setting of both E and M locomotor activities.

Neuronal feedback loop model of the SCN explains experimental results
Taken together with previous findings that AVP neurons act as the primary circadian pacesetter in vivo3,12,16,17, the above results suggest a feedback loop neural circuit of AVP and VIP neurons in the SCN (SNFL: SCN neuronal feedback loop) as a critical network machinery of the mammalian central clock (Fig. 8a), which generates robust circadian rhythms with a period of ~24 h in DD. In this context, AVP neurons are the principal oscillatory part of the SCN and regulate the circadian rhythms of VIP and other SCN cells16. AVP neurons constitute a fast oscillator with an intrinsically short period. VIP peptide, released rhythmically, acts on AVP neurons, delaying the AVP neuronal rhythm every day to lengthen its period closer to 24 h and increase its amplitude (Fig. 8a, right). In addition to this primary direct pathway, there may also be minor indirect routes through which VIP regulates AVP neurons via other SCN cells (Fig. 5). Consequently, in the absence of VIP, the AVP neuronal rhythm expresses an intrinsic short period in the attenuated behavior rhythm (Fig. 8a, middle). However, when AVP neuronal oscillation reduces its amplitude too much to control the various clock cells in the SCN, which have different cellular period lengths but an average long period, a weak long-period behavior rhythm emerges (background circadian oscillation or default clock state, discussed below in the Discussion) (Fig. 8a, left). Such rhythms also appear when the pacesetting ability of AVP neurons is impaired by specifically disrupting TTFL or blocking transmitter release. They also correlate with weak, slow Ca2+ rhythms in non-AVP cells, such as VIP neurons.

We next built a simplified mathematical model consisting of two oscillators to test if the free-running period of normal mice (i.e., the synchronized, SCN ensemble period) could be explained by the periods of AVP- and VIP-Ca2+ rhythms measured in this study (Fig. 8b and Supplementary Fig. 11). Here, the VIP-Ca2+ period represented non-AVP cells. The oscillations were obtained using a phase oscillator model with coupling31. Based on the Ca2+ rhythms in VIP-deficient mice in DD (Fig. 2a), we estimated the in vivo intrinsic period lengths of the dominant fast oscillator (i.e., AVP neurons: τA) and the presumed weak slow oscillator (non-AVP cells: τnA) to be ~22.7 h and ~24.3 h, respectively. The free-running periods of Ca2+ and the locomotor activity rhythm in control mice were ~23.7 h (Figs. 1g and 2a) and regarded as the normal SCN ensemble period.

Since AVP neurons are dominant, the coupling strength from AVP to non-AVP cells (KA→nA) should be greater than the coupling strength from non-AVP to AVP cells (KnA→A). We set KA→nA = 5x KnA→A (α=5) based on an explant study13, or 25× KnA→A (α=25) considering the reports that AVP neurons may control other SCN cells more effectively in vivo than ex vivo16,17. As in the SNFL model, we paid particular attention to the phase-delaying effect of VIP (KV) by introducing a separate term to the AVP neuronal oscillator equation. We roughly estimated that VIP is released during subjective day (CT0~12) when VIP-Ca2+ is high (Fig. 1) (red underline in Fig. 8b). Additionally, based on the phase response curves of the SCN explant PER2::LUC rhythm to VIP application32 and the behavior rhythm to in vivo optogenetic stimulation of VIP neurons33, we assumed that AVP neurons respond to VIP around CT6–CT18 (green underline in Fig. 8b) primarily by delaying their phases. Using these equations, we identified parameter ranges that produce a synchronized ensemble period of ~23.7 h (Fig. 8b, bottom). In contrast, without the additional special term (Fig. 8b, KV = 0), two oscillators synchronized; however, the resultant period remained close to the short period of the AVP neuronal oscillator and never approached the measured value of ~23.7 h when the AVP cellular oscillator dominated the non-AVP cellular oscillator (α=5 or 25).

In VIP-deficient mice, VIP’s phase-delaying effect (KV) was reduced to zero, and both AVP (KA→nA) and non-AVP (KnA→A) cellular rhythms were weakened. Nevertheless, as far as the AVP neuronal oscillator dominated the non-AVP cellular oscillator (α=5 or 25; KnA→A is not too close to zero), the two oscillators synchronized, expressing a short period close to that of the AVP cellular oscillator. However, when the AVP cellular oscillator was attenuated to the point of losing control over non-AVP cells (α and KnA→A approaching zero), AVP and non-AVP cells oscillated with different short and long periods, respectively. This is similar to what was often observed in the later stage of DD. In Avp-Vipr2−/− mice, the synchronized period was shortened due to reduced KV. In contrast, in Avp-Bmal1−/− and Avp-TeNT mice, the periods lengthened due to reduced KA→nA (i.e., α=0 or 0.2). Furthermore, this model could similarly explain the period length of Avp-CK1δ−/−; Vipwt/tTA and Avp-CK1δ−/−; ViptTA/tTA mice by just lengthening the AVP cellular intrinsic period by 1–1.5 h (Supplementary Fig. 11d).

Thus, the SNFL model may appropriately represent the logic of SCN pacesetting, both qualitatively and quantitatively.
