## Methods

Animals
Avp-Cre (C57BL/6J-Tg(Avp-icre)#Meid/Rbrc, RBRC12048) and Vip-tTA (B6(Cg)-Vipem1(tTA2)Miem/Rbrc, RBRC12109) mice were reported previously10,12. Cck-ires-Cre (Ccktm1.1(cre)Zjh/J, JAX:012706)24, Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato (Ai14)(B6.Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J, JAX:007914)27, Rosa26-LSL-SpCas9-2A-EGFP (B6J.129(B6N)-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm1(CAG-cas9*,-EGFP)Fezh/J, JAX:026175)29, Vip-ires-Cre(Viptm1(cre)Zjh/J, JAX:010908)24, CK1δ flox (B6.129S4-Csnk1dtm1Drw/J, JAX:010487)66, and Bmal1 flox (B6.129S4(Cg)-Bmal1tm1Weit/J, JAX:007668)67 mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratory. All lines were congenic on C57BL/6J. We compared the mutant mice with controls whose genetic backgrounds were comparable. Avp-Cre, Cck-ires-Cre, Vip-ires-Cre, Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato, and Rosa26-LSL-SpCas9-2A-EGFP mice were used in hemizygous or heterozygous conditions. We used both male and female mice in our experiments. Whether we pooled data from both sexes or analyzed them separately, the conclusions we reached remained almost the same. Previous studies reported slight but statistically significant sex differences in the behavior rhythms of VIP knockout mice (e.g., 0.05 h longer free-running period in females)68,69. However, the differences observed between genotypes in this study were large enough not to be affected by sex differences. The sex of individual mice is described in Supplementary Figs. and the Source Data file. Mice were maintained under a strict 12-h light/12-h dark cycle in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room and fed ad libitum. All experimental procedures involving animals were approved by the appropriate institutional animal care and use committees of Kanazawa University.

Viral vector and surgery
The AAV-2 ITR containing plasmid pGP-AAV-CAG-FLEX-jGCaMP7s-WPRE (Addgene plasmid #104495, a gift from Dr. Douglas Kim and GENIE Project)22, was obtained from Addgene. pAAV-TRE-ChR2-YFP (Addgene #171622, a gift from Hyungbae Kwon)70, was modified to construct pAAV-TRE-jRGECO1a by replacing ChR2-YFP cDNA with a jRGECO1a cDNA fragment amplified by PCR from the plasmid pAAV.CAG.-Flex.NES-jRGECO1a.WPRE.SV40 (Addgene #100852, a gift from Douglas Kim & GENIE Project)23, using the following primers: 5′-CTAGGATCCGCCACCATGCTGCAGAACGAGCTTGC-3’ and 5’-CTGAAGCTTTCACTTCGCTGTCATCATTTGTAC-3′. Then, an EcoRI-HindIII fragment of the resultant plasmid containing jRGECO1a sequence was used to replace an EcoRI-HindIII fragment containing ChrimsonR-mCherry from pAAV-TRE-ChrimsonR-mCherry (Addgene #92207, a gift from Alice Ting)71. pAAV-CAG-FLEX-taCasp3-TEVp was made by replacing a BamHI-EcoRV fragment containing EGFP of pAAV-CAG-FLEX-EGFP20 with a BamHI-EcoRV fragment containing taCasp3-TEVp from pAAV-flex-taCasp3-TEVp (Addgene #45580, a gift from Nirao Shah & Jim Wells)72. pAAV-U6-gVipr2-EF1α-DIO-mCherry, a plasmid for CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Vipr2 gene disruption, was generated as follows. The target sites for CRISPR-Cas9 were designed by CRISPOR73. Two sequences targeting Vipr2 gene were selected: 5′-TGCTGGCGCCCGGCAGACGT-3′ and 5′-CCAGATTTCATAGATGCGTG-3′. Oligonucleotides encoding the guide sequences were cloned into the BbsI and BsaI sites of pX333 (Addgene #64073, a gift from Dr. Andrea Ventura)74. Then, a fragment containing two tandem units of U6-gRNA was amplified by PCR, using the following primers: 5′-agtacgcgTCGAGCATGCTCGAGAATGG-3′ and 5′-agtacgcgtCGGGTACCCCATTTGTCTGC-3′, and cloned into the MluI site of pAAV-EF1a-DIO-mCherry (a gift from Dr. Bryan Roth) as described previously75. pAAV-U6-gControl-EF1α-DIO-mCherry contains spacer sequences from pX333 instead of gRNA sequences for Vipr2. pAAV-EF1α-DIO-GFP::TeNT was kindly provided by Dr. Richard D. Palmiter76.

Recombinant AAV vectors (AAV2-rh10) were produced using a triple-transfection, helper-free method and purified as described previously12. Briefly, 293A cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were transfected with pHelper (Stratagene), pAAV2-rh10 (provided by Penn Vector Core), and one of AAV-2 ITR containing plasmids using a standard calcium phosphate method. Three days later, the transfected cells were collected and suspended in PBS containing 1 mM MgCl2. After 2 freeze-thaw cycles, the cell lysate was treated with benzonase nuclease (Merck) at 37 °C for 30 min, and centrifuged 2 times at 16,000 × g for 10 min. The supernatant was used as the virus-containing solution. The titers of recombinant AAV vectors were determined by quantitative PCR: AAV-CAG-DIO-jGCaMP7s, 3.4×1013; AAV-TRE-jRGECO1a, 8.6×1012; AAV-CAG-FLEX-taCasp3-TEVp, 5.7×1012; AAV-CAG-FLEX-nls-mCherry, 6.1×1012; AAV-U6-gVipr2-EF1α-DIO-mCherry, 6.8×1012; AAV-U6-gControl-EF1α-DIO-mCherry, 2.6×1012; AAV-EF1α-DIO-GFP::TeNT, 1.8×1012 and AAV-CAG-FLEX-EGFP, 1.0×1013 genome copies/ml. Stereotaxic injection of AAV vectors was performed as described previously12. Two weeks or immediately after surgery, we began monitoring the mice for their locomotor activity.

In vivo fiber photometry
We used 8 Avp-Cre; ViptTA/tTA, 6 Cckwt/ires-Cre; ViptTA/tTA, 8 control (5 Avp-Cre; Vipwt/tTA and 3 Cckwt/ires-Cre; Vipwt/tTA), and 6 Avp-Bmal1−/−×Vip-tTA (Avp-Cre; Bmal1flox/flox; Vipwt/tTA) mice. Mice were anesthetized by administering a cocktail of medetomidine (0.3 mg/kg), midazolam (4 mg/kg), and butorphanol (5 mg/kg) and were secured to the stereotaxic apparatus (Muromachi Kikai). Lidocaine (1%) was applied for local anesthesia before making the surgical incision. We drilled a small hole in the exposed region of the skull using a dental drill. We injected 1.0 μL of the mixture of AAV-CAG-FLEX-jGCaMP7s and AAV-TRE-jRGECO1a (ratio 1:1, flow rate=0.1 μL/min) into the right SCN (posterior: 0.5 mm, lateral: 0.25 mm, depth: 5.7 mm from the bregma) with a 33G Hamilton syringe (1701RN Neuros Syringe, Hamilton) to label AVP and VIP neurons. We then placed an implantable optical fiber (400 μm core, N.A. 0.39, 6 mm, ferrule 2.5 mm, Thorlabs or RWD) above the SCN (posterior: 0.2 mm, lateral: 0.2 mm, depth: 5.3 mm from the bregma) with dental cement (Super-bond C&B, Sun Medical). The dental cement was painted black. Atipamezole (0.3 mg/kg) was administered postoperatively to shorten the anesthetized period. Mice were used for experiments 2–7 weeks after the virus injection and optical fiber implantation. Their ages ranged from 3 to 10 months, including both males and females.

A fiber photometry system (FP3002, Neurophotometrics) was used to record the calcium signal of SCN neurons in freely moving mice77,78. Excitation light sources were a 470-nm LED for detecting Ca2+-dependent jGCaMP7s fluorescence signal (F470), a 560-nm LED for detecting Ca2+-dependent jRGECO1a fluorescence signal (F560), and a 415-nm LED for Ca2+-independent isosbestic fluorescence signal (F415). The duration of the excitation lights was 50 ms, and the onsets of the excitation timing of the LEDs were interleaved. The lights passed through excitation bandpass filters, dichroic mirrors, and then to the animal via fiber-optic patch cords (BBP(4)_400/440/900-0.37_1m_FCM-4xFCM_LAF, MFP_400/440/LWMJ-0.37_1m_FCM-ZF2.5_LAF, Doric Lenses) and the implanted optical fiber. Subsequently, all signals were detected using a CMOS camera through the optical fibers, dichroic mirrors, and emission bandpass filters. The green emission signal and the red emission signal were recorded separately and simultaneously. Ca2+ signals were recorded every 10 min for 30 s using Bonsai software at a sampling rate of 6.6 Hz for each color. The excitation intensities of the 470-nm, 560-nm, and 415-nm LEDs at the tip of the patch cord on the animal side ranged from 60 to 120 μw. During recording, the mouse was housed in a 12-h light–dark cycle for more than 7 days (LD condition) and then transferred to continuous darkness for more than 21 days (DD condition) in a custom-made acrylic cage surrounded by a sound-attenuating chamber.

Ratio (R) was defined as the ratio between F470 and F415 in green channel (F470/F415green) or the ratio between F560 and F415 in red channel (F560/F415red) for calibration and reducing motion artifacts. R was averaged within a 30-s session20. To detrend the gradual decrease of the signal during the recording days, ±12 h average from the time (145 points) was calculated as baseline (R0). The data were subsequently detrended by the subtraction of R0 (ΔR). Then, the ΔR/R0 value was calculated. To determine the daily peak phase of jGCaMP7s or jRGECO1a Ca2+ signal, ΔR/R0 were smoothened with a 21-point moving average, then the middle of the time points crossing value 0 upward (Ca2+ onset) and downward (Ca2+ offset) were defined as the midpoint that reflects the peak phases. Additionally, the intervals between two adjacent midpoints were defined as the daily periods (Fig. 1f, g)12. Because VIP-Ca2+ rhythm in VIP deficient mice attenuated drastically in DD, we failed to determine its Ca2+ onset, offset, and daily period at the late stage. A double-plotted actogram of the jGCaMP7s or jRGECO1a signal was prepared by converting all ΔR/R0 to positive values by subtracting the minimum value of ΔR/R0. Subsequently, these values were multiplied by 100 or 1000 and rounded off. The plots were made via ClockLab (Actimetrics) with normalization in each row to emphasize weak VIP-Ca2+ and CCK-Ca2+ rhythmicity in VIP-deficient mice at the late stage in DD. To quantitively analyze the weak rhythms and their changes, periods and amplitudes of Ca2+ signals (ΔR/R0) were calculated by periodogram with 10-min bins for all three weeks and shifting five-day time windows in DD, respectively (Figs. 2, 4, and 6; Supplementary Figs. 1, 2, 5, and 9).

During the fiber photometry recordings, the animal’s locomotor activity was monitored using an infrared sensor (AMN31112 and Arduino) in 10-min bins. A double-plotted actogram of locomotor activity was also prepared and overlaid on that of the jGCaMP7s and jRGECO1a signal. The onset of locomotor activity was determined using the actograms. Initially, we attempted to automatically detect the onset; however, it was followed by a manual visual inspection and modifications by the experimenter. The intervals between two adjacent locomotor onsets were defined as the daily periods (Fig. 1f, g). To calculate the CT of the midpoint phases of jGCaMP7s and jRGECO1a signals, we have defined the regression line of locomotor activity onsets as CT12. Period and amplitude of locomotor activity were also calculated by χ2 periodogram analyses for all days or 5 consecutive days in DD to analyze weak rhythmicity of VIP-deficient mice (Figs. 2, 4, and 6; Supplementary Figs. 1, 2, and 5).

We confirmed the jGCaMP7s and jRGECO1a expressions and the position of the optical fiber by slicing the brains into 30 μm coronal sections using a cryostat (Leica). The sections were mounted on glass slides with a mounting medium (VECTASHIELD HardSet with DAPI, H-1500, Vector Laboratories; Dako Fluorescence Mounting Medium, Agilent Technologies) and observed via epifluorescence microscope (BZ-9000, Keyence).

Behavioral analyses
Male and female Avp-CK1δ−/−; ViptTA/tTA (Avp-Cre; CK1δflox/flox; ViptTA/tTA) or control (Avp-Cre; CK1δflox/flox; Vipwt/tTA) (Fig. 2), Vip-Casp3 (Vipwt/ires-Cre mice injected bilaterally with AAV-CAG-FLEX-taCasp3-TEVp) or control (Vipwt/ires-Cre mice injected with AAV-CAG-FLEX-nls-mCherry and wild type C57BL/6J mice injected with AAV-CAG-FLEX-taCasp3-TEVp) (Supplementary Fig. 7), Avp-Vipr2−/− (Avp-Cre; Rosa26-LSL-Cas9-2A-EGFP mice injected bilaterally with AAV-U6-gVipr2-EF1α-DIO-mCherry) or control (Avp-Cre; Rosa26-LSL-Cas9-2A-EGFP mice injected with AAV-U6-gControl-EF1a-DIO-mCherry) (Fig. 5), and Avp-TeNT (Avp-Cre mice injected bilaterally with AAV-EF1α-DIO-GFP::TeNT) or control (Avp-Cre mice injected with AAV-CAG-FLEX-EGFP) (Fig. 7) mice, aged 8 to 30 weeks, were housed individually in a cage placed in a light-tight chamber (light intensity was approximately 100 lux). Spontaneous locomotor activity (home-cage activity) was monitored by infrared motion sensors (O’Hara) in 1-min bins with a custom-made program as described previously12. Actogram, activity profile, and χ2 periodogram analyses were performed via ClockLab (Actimetrics). The free-running period and amplitude were measured by periodogram for all days in DD (Avp-CK1δ−/−; ViptTA/tTA and Avp-TeNT) or the last 14 days in DD (Vip-Casp3). In the case of Avp-Vipr2−/− and control mice, their periods and amplitudes were measured by periodogram for 10 days in 1st or 2nd stage in DD (Fig. 5).

Immunohistochemistry
Immunostaining was performed as described previously10,12,75. Mice were killed approximately at ZT2 by transcardial perfusion of PBS followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS. For estimating co-expression of CCK and AVP, Cck-ires-Cre; Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato mice were pretreated with intracerebroventricular injections of colchicine (40 µg in 1 µl saline) 48 h before perfusion around ZT6. Then, the mice brains were postfixed in the 4% PFA at 4˚C overnight, followed by immersion in 30% sucrose solution at 4°C for 2 days. Serial coronal brain sections (30 μm thickness) were made with a cryostat (CM1860, Leica) and collected in 4 series—one of which was further immunostained. For immunofluorescence staining, sections were washed with PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 (PBST) and blocked with PBST plus 3% BSA (blocking solution). Then, slices were incubated overnight with the designated primary antibodies in the blocking solution at 4°C. Antibodies used were rabbit anti-GFP antibody (1:1000; A11122, Thermo Fisher Scientific), rabbit anti-VIP antibody (1:1,000; #20077, Immunostar), rabbit anti-AVP antibody (Millipore, 1:2000), and rabbit anti-VPAC2 antibody (Abcam, 1:1000). Then, slices were washed with PBST, followed by incubation with the designated secondary antibodies in blocking solution for 4 h. Secondary antibodies used in this study were Alexa Fluor 488–conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:2000, A-21206; Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 594–conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:2000, A-21207; Thermo Fisher Scientific), and Alexa Fluor 647–conjugated goat anti-Rabbit IgG antibody (1:600, 111-605-003; Jackson Immuno Research Laboratories). After incubation with secondary antibody, slices were washed with PBS, mounted on slide glasses, air dried, and coverslipped using Mounting Medium (H-1500, Vector Laboratories; Dako Fluorescence Mounting Medium, Agilent Technologies). Images were taken using an epifluorescence microscope (BZ-9000, Keyence) or a confocal microscope (Fluoview Fv10i, Olympus). Fluorescent signal of Alexa Fluor 647 was pseudo-colored in light blue (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 7). The VPAC2 expression levels were quantified by ImageJ as follows (Fig. 5b). First, the mean intensities of pixels within the ROIs in the SCN shell and core were calculated. Then, the values of the region lateral to the SCN were regarded as background and were subtracted from those of the SCN.

Mathematical model construction and simulation
The two-oscillator model with coupling was modified by introducing a term in which VIP neurons delay the phase of AVP neuron oscillator31, reflecting the phase-dependent receptivity of AVP to VIP’s delaying effect.

dθA/dt = ωA + KnA→A sin(θnA − θA) − KV * max(sin(θnA), 0) * max(sin(θA − δ), 0)

dθnA/dt = ωnA + KA→nA sin(θA − θnA)

where θA, θnA denote the phases of oscillator A (representing AVP neurons) and oscillator nA (non-AVP neurons, including VIP neurons), respectively. ωA, ωnA are the intrinsic angular velocities (ωA = 2π/τA, ωnA = 2π/τnA), and τA, τnA are the intrinsic periods (τA = 22.7 h, except for Supplementary Fig. 11d where τA = 23.7 h; τnA = 24.3 h), based on the AVP-Ca2+ and VIP-Ca2+ fiber photometry results presented in this study. KnA→A denotes the coupling strength from oscillator nA to A, KA→nA denotes the coupling strength from oscillator A to nA, and KV represents inhibitory modulation (e.g., VIP-mediated inhibition), which is active only when sin(θnA) > 0 and sin(θA − δ) > 0. δ represents the phase difference between oscillator A and its receptivity, and was set to π/2 (Fig. 8b), 0 (Supplementary Fig. 11a), π (Supplementary Fig. 11b), or 3π/2 (Supplementary Fig. 11c). The ratio between KA→nA and KnA→A (α) was set to 0, 0.2, 1, 5, and 25. In the heatmaps, gray regions indicate simulations in which a stable period could not be determined, whereas black regions indicate the final periods between oscillators A and nA are different (>0.2 h). All simulations were performed in MATLAB.

Statistical analysis
All results are expressed as mean±SEM. Statistical analyses were performed using Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad). For comparisons of 2 groups, two-tailed unpaired Student’s or Welch’s t tests were performed. For comparisons of multiple groups with no difference of variance by Bartlett test, two-way repeated measures ANOVA followed by Bonferroni, Tukey or Holm-Sidak post hoc test were performed. For circular data, Rayleigh test, Watson–Williams test, and Harrison–Kanji test were performed with Circstat MATLAB Toolbox for Circular Statistics79. All p values less than 0.05 were considered as statistically significant. Only relevant information from the statistical analysis was indicated in the text and figures. Detailed results of the statistical analyses are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

### Reviewer 1

How the 20,000 neurons and astrocytes of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) generate a stable ~24 hours (circadian) signal is an important area of study because this property determines the temporal pattern of our behavior and physiology. In this study, Wang et al. use an impressive range of intersectional manipulations and long-term in vivo Ca-imaging to explore how two distinct cell groups of the SCN, those expressing arginine vasopressin (AVP) and those expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interact to main robust rhythmicity. They conclude that “the neuronal feedback circuit composed of AVP cellular oscillator and VIP peptide signaling is crucial for the robust circadian rhythm.”
I have two significant thoughts about his study. First, the impressive technical features of in vivo cell-specific imaging have already been published by this group, including the excellent paper by Tsuno et al, PLOS Biology, 2023. This reduces some of the immediate impact of the study. Second, the conclusion could have been made before this work was conducted. There is an extensive literature, again some of it from this group, about the role of AVP neurons in driving circadian behavior and of the requirement for VIP signaling to sustain the SCN clockwork. The real question to be answered is how do AVP and VIP cells do what they do - what are the mechanisms? It is not clear to me how this study moves towards a substantial answer, but the Authors may be able to articulate how their results do push things forward by elucidating “the mechanism of how VIP regulates the cellular clocks of AVP neurons”.
1. Figures 1 & 2 show how Ca2+ rhythms in SCN VIP and AVP cells relate to each other and to behavioral rhythms in wild-type mice, and then how these relationships possibly change in the VIP-deficient ViptTA mouse. Specifically, it shows that loss of VIP reduces the amplitude and shortens the period of AVP Ca rhythms and, in parallel, is associated with disrupted behavioral activity rhythms with overall shortened period.
Even under LD the Ca rhythms of AVP cells are diminished in VIP-null mice. This is an interesting result because it indicates that, in the absence of VIP, light cannot boost the AVP Ca rhythms. Thus, loss of normal VIP signaling affects the SCN circuit properties and the period of AVP cells.
In the absence of VIP, Ca rhythms in VIP cells remain robustly light-driven but disappear very rapidly on transfer to DD. Why might VIP cells be sensitive to loss of VIP because scRNAseq has shown that they do not express Vipr2? The Authors suggest this is an indirect result of the weaker and faster AVP cell rhythms in VIP-null mice, hence the common period of 23.67 hours for AVP and VIP cells.
In the final stages of the study, however, VIP cells are reported to show a longer period of 24.33 hours in VIP-null mice. I do not fully understand, however, how the VIP Ca rhythms were analysed. In Figure 1d, e, it petered out after 1 week of DD but in Figure 2 parameters are calculated until days 16 -20. Is it not possible that these parameter values are meaningless because the rhythms have become so poorly defined? A value may be calculated for period, but it will come with an error term that may render it not biologically meaningful. Similarly, the periodograms in Figure 2a suggest a dual periodicity (early and later?) for VIP Ca rhythms – but how these were calculated and analysed statistically is not clear. The time-series plots in Figure 2c show the evolution of the longer period, but the point remains that these rhythms were very poorly defined and so how much relevance can be placed on this apparent change in period? In addition, in the moving time series, the same data points are used repeatedly, and then ANOVA is applied to the means for each 5 days value. I am unclear as to whether this is appropriate as the measures are not independent, for example 5-9 shares 4 values of 6-10.
A final query is why does the later behavioral period track the presumed late period of the VIP and not the period of the AVP cells (Figure 2c) if AVP cells are the pacesetters? Over the 20 days of recording the amplitude and period of AVP cells are unchanged and so it might be expected that their influence over behavior would also be maintained.
In the later stages of recording are we simply looking at some non-specific associations in a clock that is progressively falling apart: behavioral offsets could not even be defined in the VIP-null mice? In the early stages of DD, where measurements are much more robust, AVP and VIP cells behave similarly.
I have a technical question regarding the individual period values. Is there some aspect of the periodogram which causes it to deliver particular fractional values? For example, Figure 2a has .67 (2/3) and .33 (1/3), as does Figure 3e, alongside .50 (1/2). To what degree does the doublet for period in VIP-null animals apply to individual animals and to what degree is it a population measure?
“These results suggest that VIP neurons may be a subordinate slow oscillator and exhibit a weak, long-period rhythm that correlates with the behavior rhythm in vivo when the AVP cellular rhythm is attenuated by VIP deficiency.”
Alternatively, it may be that the loss of VIP in some way alters the intrinsic properties of VIP cells. Moreover, the Authors do not consider whether changes in the Ca rhythms are a result of altered behavioral rhythms and not a cause of them.
2. To test whether the VIP-null compromise of AVP (shorter period) and VIP cell (short then long period) rhythms is generalisable across the SCN, Figure 3 describes Ca2+ rhythms in SCN CCK cells and the impact of VIP deletion on them. Again, elegant intersectional approaches are deployed. In control mice, the CCK cells exhibit a Ca rhythm, as reported previously. The VIP-null phenotype of VIP cells was replicated with an independent cohort of mice. Note, is this assumed independence correct, even though the mice again had identical periods of 22.67 h and 24.33 h (see technical comment above re. periodogram)? In VIP-null mice the rhythms are initially light-driven and then damp rapidly on transfer to DD. They do lengthen, but not to the extent seen in Figure 1, raising uncertainly about the robustness of the late VIP-null phenotype.
The Ca rhythms of CCK cells in VIP-null mice were light-driven on LD and showed rapid damping in DD, replicating the phenotype of VIP cells. They do not, however, show a late lengthened period, as the VIP cells did, so they are a half-way house. The statistical comparisons are pretty weak, however, and again suffer from the poor definition/ high variance of rhythms in the later stages. The Authors conclude that “CCK-Ca2+ rhythm is weak and unstable and has more heterogeneous periods in VIP deficiency. Such heterogeneity may partly reflect that CCK neurons contain at least two subpopulations, one overlapping with a small subpopulation of AVP neurons.” This is speculation. Fundamentally in the absence of VIP the SCN cellular rhythms are low amplitude (AVP) or damped poorly defined period (VIP, CCK).
3. Given the importance of VIP when absent throughout development, the Authors then explore the effect of adult-restricted loss of the VIP cells. A different mouse line, heterozygous VIP IRES Cre received AAV injection of Cre-dependent caspase. Post-mortem staining revealed absence of VIP, and the mice exhibited a short period of 22.9 hours. Unfortunately, there are no control animals in this experiment: for example, injected with control AAV or mice not of the IRES-CRE background and injected with AAV conditional caspase. The data are therefore incomplete, and this particular study would require expansion to be suitable for publication.
4. To complement the examination of VIP-deficiency, the Authors then deleted its receptor, Vipr2, from AVP cells by cell-specific expression of Cre-conditional CAS9 and AAV inject of sgRNA. (Figure 4) This is, again, a technically impressive approach although targeting was confirmed by mCherry and GFP signals but levels of Vipr2 were not determined. This targeting caused an acute shortening of period, compared to mice injected with control AAV, but given the impact of genomic ablation of Vipr2 (short period and/ or highly disturbed activity rhythms and a desynchronised SCN) it is surprising that the phenotype is so modest. Despite the short period, the activity patterns are robust, and behavioral period is recovered after ~ 3weeks. This was repeated in a second cohort of ice – something changes ~21 days after injection. In the absence of validation of the deletion of Vipr2, it is difficult to interpret these data.
The Authors state that: “These observations suggest the indirect pathways in the regulation of AVP neurons by VIP neurons that may be involved in the compensatory recovery of the standard period in Avp-Vipr2−/− mice.” This is highly speculative.
5. Having targetted Vipr2 in AVP cells, the Authors then tested the effect of Bmal1 deletion in AVP cells on behavior and VIP and AVP cell Ca rhythms. On my reading, there is no control group in this experiment: all mice were AVP-Bmal1 null? This confounds any interpretation of the phenotypes observed: period, duration of Ca elevation etc.
Notably, the targetted animals exhibited a longer period, 24.17 h, but this is far off the original report of 24.8 +0.1 hours in Mieda et al 2015. And again, a single period is given but with no error terms to mirror its variance between mice.
The Authors note that: “As expected, the AVP-Ca2+ exhibited little circadian rhythmicity, although this might be due to low jGCaMP7s expression in TTFL-deficient AVP neurons.” So, is the rhythm correctly reported or not? It is very clear that robust VIP cell Ca rhythms are maintained, again with an identical period to behavior, 24.17 hours. So ostensibly, when AVP cells have no TTFL, VIP cells can nevertheless drive circadian behavior?
6. In the final element of the study, the Authors blocked neurotransmitter release from AVP cells by injecting Cre-dependent AAV TeNT, or AAV EGFP as a control. This caused a clear and unequivocal lengthening of period (~24.5 hours) when compared to controls (~23.2 hours). This is again interpreted as the effect of releasing the SCN from its dominance by the intrinsically short-period oscillator of AVP cells. There are also interesting aspects of the relative movements of “evening” and “morning” activity bouts, and the phenotype chimes very well, as noted by the Authors, with AVP-Bmal1 null and AVP-Vgat null.
7. “Our results reveal a feedback loop neuronal circuit of these two neuron types that may be the essential network mechanism of the SCN central circadian pacemaker.”
The conclusion is an extension of the literature, but this proposal fails to indicate mechanisms. The nature of the loop is not specified: what is its structure and topology, and how might it sit with regard to other SCN circuit components? There is a sense of playing “whack a mole” insofar as when reasoning from VIP cells to AVP cells or vice versa, additional unknown and indirect elements have to be hypothesised to fill the gaps such that the identity to the relevant circuit elements is never pinned down.
8. On a general point to facilitate presentation, I suggest that the figures and text should be rearranged in order to report on control conditions first (placed to the left and at the top of figures) and then say how experimental groups (placed to the right and at the bottom) compared with controls.

### Reviewer 2

The study applied dual-color fiber photometry recording to VIP-deficient mice, allowing them to simultaneously monitor the cellular circadian rhythms from two types of SCN neurons. They analyzed the circadian behavior rhythms of multiple mouse strains that had various impairments in the communication between VIP and AVP neurons.
This is an extremely elegant and complex genetic approach, to disrupt VIP (and other) signaling while performing dual-color Ca2+ fiber photometry. The technological approach is very impressive. The results are complex. One caveat that should be, and is, addressed in the text is that the assumption that the populations of VIP and AVP (and CCK) cells are internally coherent, especially during disruption of normal signaling, may not be true. For example see https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2209329120. Plus, recent snRNAseq studies have shown that VIP+ and AVP+ populations are internally diverse. Therefore, treating them as distinct groups may be an oversimplification. I don’t suggest that it invalidates these results, just that it should be clearly acknowledged that there is likely more complexity/diversity among cells and across days. The beginning of the discussion does acknowledge this, which is good, as it is a key point.
The results are, generally, wide in terms of # of manipulations, but shallow, in terms of #s of mice or depth of understanding of the system, derived from a disrupting VIP signaling, blocking the TTFL in cell subtypes, etc. Studying the coupled system in vivo, while it is broken, is tough to do before we understand how it works when it isn’t broken. The discussion reveals that the paper raises way more questions than it can answer. Overall this is a technical tour de force, with rather limited new insight achieved. No new conceptual model is provided that can help us understand this circuit better than we already did.

### Reviewer 3

Summary of the key results
The researchers investigated the role AVP neurons play in SCN regulation. They hypothesize that VIP -> AVP communication plays a role in circadian rhythm, given that the TTFL loop in VIP neurons is weaker compared to that in AVP neurons. The research shows that AVP neurons are the principal oscillators with an intrinsically short period. It strengthens previous observations by this research group. When the internal clock of AVP neurons is disrupted by Bmal1 KO or their communication with other neurons is removed with TeNT, the rhythm becomes longer than 24 hours. These results shed interesting new light on the role of AVP neurons.
I think the interpretation of some unique features that appeared in the results could be claimed in a better way if additional data will be considered and presented, as listed below.
Originality and significance:
The paper, as indicated in the discussion, is the first to use fiberphotometry with 2-colors in the SCN in vivo. The paper nicely combines genetic manipulation and AAV-based technologies (such as CRISPR) with calcium imaging and LMA (locomotor activity) detection. Furthermore, the paper’s significance lies in the in vivo monitoring of AVP-related features. The fact that in vivo effects are different from slices is critical here, as the SCN and AVP neurons also get inputs from the surrounding, which was not tested or discussed here, which is a weakness of the paper.
The paper aims to understand the communication mechanism, but it lacks a clear model, or at least it is not represented in a clear way. To specify, the fact that AVP is a short-period pacemaker is well explained and demonstrated, but the interpretation of the changes in the LMA split or VIP calcium imaging after 3 weeks is not strongly convincing. An additional figure that shows the model will be a great addition.
Data & methodology:
1. The combined usage of calcium imaging, LMA detection, and cell manipulation using AAV is impressive. The data analysis is straightforward, but could benefit from a more advanced analysis, which will highlight the dual activity along the day, such as Rayleigh plots, as presented in Supp. Figure 2.
2. In the paper by Wen et. al. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-020-0586-x) it was shown that Cck neurons are divided into two subpopulations, one is rhythmic Cck+/C1ql3+ and one is less (Cck+/Bdnf+). Did you try to identify which subpopulation was located under the fiber? See, for example, https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(21)01197-9, or even regular slice histology. This could shed light on the effect found in vivo.
3. The low number of animals in Figure 5 (n=3) makes it hard to interpret the results.
4. The results under DD conditions in the manipulated animals are interpreted as a phase-delaying model, and the two oscillators option is declined by considering a few aspects. However, I suggest that the new LMA pattern suggests split SCN activity (Figure 4). It was found in hamsters https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11760012/, and was identified as a split SCN activity by https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.290.5492.799.
I would be interested in seeing circadian clock gene expression during different time points throughout the day. Is the expression even on both sides of the SCN under DD?
5. When genetic cell manipulation was used using AAV (Figure 4, Figure 6), did you check if the results depend on the virus injection spread pattern? Was one side of the SCN better expressed by the virus compared to the other? The quality of the injection (with reference to Right/Left) vs. the effect should be quantified, and the interpretation should include this information.
6. It is not clear to me why the initial hypothesis is that the prevention of the neurotransmitters' release (Figure 6) would lengthen the period. I would expect it will prevent cell-cell communication and will cause asynchrony, which will show unsynchronized LMAs at DD, when there is no entrainment. I would further claim that the diversity in the results could be due to Right/Left expression of the virus. The histology of AAV efficiency in each mouse should be determined and presented in correlation to the effect.
